newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: ZEMAN WANTS PARLIAMENTS IN ON CZECH-GERMAN PACT.
newsitem.headline: ZEMAN WANTS PARLIAMENTS IN ON CZECH-GERMAN PACT.

text.p: Czech Social Democrat leader and parliament chairman Milos Zeman on Friday insisted that Czech and German legislatures should play a large role in approving a long-awaited pact aimed at closing the book on World War Two.

Zeman told a news conference that the parliaments have a right to alter the declaration's government-negotiated text, which addresses the Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and subsequent expulsion of 2.5 million ethnic Germans.
"Our common interest in the declaration should be showed by (the fact that) the parliaments of the two countries will negotiate it as well," said Zeman.
"It is not an international treaty... the decision made is not just yes or no," he added.

Both governments were trying to agree on the text of the declaration long before Czech general elections in June this year, but a final agreement was postponed to avoid involvment of the sensitive issue in the campaign.

Zeman's party fared unexpectedly well in the June elections, stripping the centre-right coalition of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus of its majority in the parliament, and gaining Zeman and his party a major role in the house.

The declaration seeks to address Czech memories of the 1938-1945 Nazi occupation, and German memories of the indiscriminate expulsion of the Sudeten Germans for supporting Hitler, authorised by the victorious World War Two allies.
Zeman told the Czech daily Pravo earlier this week the main problem may be how to describe the Sudetens' removal.

Prague wants the word "transfer" which is used in the 1945 Potsdam agreement when the victorious World War Two allies authorised the former Czechoslovakia to throw out the Sudetens. Bonn is believed to want a stronger word such as expulsion.
"We were assured that the declaration is rather of a morally-political character than a strictly legal document which would directly bind both sides," he added.
The talks on the pact got a boost when Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in September he would like to have it approved by the year's end.
Czech President Vaclav Havel then said after meeting coalition and opposition leaders earlier this month that more talks were still needed.
The Czech Republic is the only remaining victim of Nazi occupation not to have come to terms with Germany.

Negotiations on the declaration have dragged on for more than a year, hampered by political pressures particularly from Sudeten Germans and their decendents now living in Southern Germany who are demanding compensation from the Prague government.
